title: Decommissioning Enterprise Software: AI Agents and the Collapse of the Replication Moat
content: I have spent the last six years building software for a living. For most of that time, one rule held: if a company bought a big piece of business software, it was stuck with it, because rebuilding that software would cost far more than just paying for it year after year. This paper is about why that rule is breaking. With an AI coding assistant that costs a few hundred dollars a month, tools that can take apart almost any program, and open models you can run on your own hardware, a single developer can now rebuild the part of a product that a business actually uses, in weeks instead of years. I walk through three real cases from October 2026, the plain economics behind them, what the law does and does not protect, why hiding how your systems work no longer keeps them safe, and who ends up controlling these tools. I am not saying software has lost its value. I am saying the industry can no longer charge people for how hard it is to leave, and the change is going to be messy.
